module_title: Intermediary Liability, SDFs, and Cross-Border Transfers
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams, corporate litigators, and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the complex Safe Harbour protections under the IT Act, the heavy compliance burdens on Significant Data Fiduciaries (SDFs), and the severe penalty adjudication framework of the DPDPA.

core_concepts.title: Intermediary Liability & Safe Harbour (Section 79, IT Act)
core_concepts.description:
An 'Intermediary' (like WhatsApp, Google, or an ISP) simply receives, stores, or transmits records on behalf of another person.
- The Safe Harbour Rule: Under Section 79, an intermediary is NOT liable for third-party information or data made available by them, provided they: (1) merely act as a conduit, (2) do not initiate or modify the transmission, and (3) observe 'due diligence' guidelines issued by the Central Government.
- Exception: The protection drops immediately if they fail to expeditiously remove unlawful material after receiving 'actual knowledge' (usually a court order or government notification).

core_concepts.title: Significant Data Fiduciaries (SDFs)
core_concepts.description:
Under the DPDPA, the Central Government designates certain entities as SDFs based on the volume of data processed, sensitivity, and risk to electoral democracy or national security.
- Extra Obligations: SDFs face massive regulatory burdens. They must: (1) Appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO) based in India, (2) Appoint an Independent Data Auditor, and (3) Conduct periodic Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA).

core_concepts.title: Cross-Border Data Transfers: The 'Blacklist' Approach
core_concepts.description:
A radical departure from global norms (like Europe's GDPR).
- The GDPR uses a 'Whitelist' approach (data can only go to pre-approved safe countries). 
- The DPDPA uses a **'Blacklist'** approach. Personal data can flow freely to any country in the world, EXCEPT for specific countries explicitly restricted (blacklisted) by the Central Government through notification. This highly liberalized approach favors tech innovation and global business.

core_concepts.title: Penalties and the Adjudication Hierarchy
core_concepts.description:
The DPDPA decriminalized data privacy. There are NO prison sentences, only massive financial penalties designed as deterrents.
- Penalties: Up to **₹250 Crore** for failing to take reasonable security safeguards. Up to ₹200 Crore for failing to notify a data breach.
- Appellate Hierarchy: Decisions of the DPBI are appealed to the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal **(TDSAT)**. Appeals against TDSAT orders go directly to the **Supreme Court of India**.

important_entities.name: State Exemptions (Section 17, DPDPA)
important_entities.significance: The Central Government can exempt any of its instrumentalities from the Act's provisions in the interests of sovereignty, national security, maintaining public order, or preventing incitement to an offense. This remains the most heavily criticized aspect of the DPDPA by privacy advocates.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Advanced exams constantly test this: 'Under the DPDPA, if a tech company leaks your data, the Data Protection Board will order them to pay you ₹50 Lakhs in compensation.' **FALSE**. The DPDPA removed the statutory right to claim direct damages/compensation from the Board (which previously existed under the IT Act Sec 43A). The massive ₹250 Cr penalties are paid to the State (Consolidated Fund of India), not to the victim.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember that an SDF must uniquely have a Data Protection Officer (DPO), an Independent Auditor, and conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA) [1.1.2].

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Law Optional or Mains GS-2, when evaluating India's data regime, you MUST contrast the DPDPA's liberal **'Blacklist' cross-border transfer model** against the GDPR's restrictive 'Whitelist' model [1.1.3].
